report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is broadly supported, but the benefit is modest and should not be interpreted as proof that anti-cytokine drugs are depression treatments in their own right.

The strongest evidence is a 2016 systematic review/meta-analysis of clinical trials in chronic inflammatory illnesses in which depressive symptoms were secondary outcomes. It found that cytokine-targeting treatment was associated with improvement in depressive symptoms versus control. Importantly, the authors examined whether this simply tracked improvement in physical disease and did not find a clear relationship—supporting, but not proving, a direct mood-related effect.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27752078/  
https://api.repository.cam.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/26e034db-38b4-4fe0-8b5e-c0d3fb97312f/content

A subsequent large placebo-controlled “mega-analysis” pooling trial data across inflammatory disorders also reported antidepressant effects of immunomodulatory drugs. The design strengthens the conclusion because it compares drugs with placebo and standardizes symptom effects across studies.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7244402/  
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-019-0471-8

**Key limitations:** Most participants were treated for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, or inflammatory bowel disease—not primarily for diagnosed major depressive disorder. Depression measures were often secondary outcomes, and reduced pain, disability, fatigue, and inflammation may all improve mood. Effects may differ by drug target, illness, baseline inflammatory status, and whether someone has clinical depression.

Thus, anti-cytokine therapy can plausibly reduce depressive symptoms *when appropriately prescribed for a chronic inflammatory condition*, but evidence does not justify using these immunosuppressive drugs solely to treat depression outside research or specialist care.
